strengths: The paper develops a clean and well-organized measure-based framework for single-layer softmax attention that unifies finite- and infinite-prompt analysis, and clearly articulates when softmax attention effectively becomes linear (Lemma 2.1 for Gaussian inputs).

The concentration results (Propositions 3.1 and 3.4) cover both the attention output and its gradients w.r.t. the trainable parameters in L2, which the authors convincingly argue is essential for training-dynamics results and goes beyond the concurrent moment-only analysis of Bohbot et al. (2025). The proof strategy (handling heavy-tailed exp(z'Uz) weights via a convex-hull/max-inequality argument on the exceptional event, with case analysis on the query norm) is careful and non-trivial.

Theorem 4.3 is a genuinely useful transfer principle: it converts analyses of infinite-prompt (linearized) attention dynamics into risk guarantees for finite-prompt softmax attention, providing a reusable toolkit rather than a one-off result.

As an application, Theorem 5.2 establishes convergence to Bayes-optimal risk for in-context linear regression with softmax attention under anisotropic Gaussian covariates, extending Chen et al. (2024) which is restricted to isotropic covariates, while using comparatively simpler proof machinery (adaptation of Zhang et al. 2024).

The treatment of limitations is honest and thoughtful: Remark 3.2 addresses the query-token autocorrelation discrepancy with practical attention, Remark 5.3 discusses the absence of explicit convergence rates and degenerate-covariance extensions, and Assumption 5.1 is correctly flagged as mainly technical.

Reproducibility is good: code is publicly available, full experimental details (learning rate, batch size, seeds, hardware, runtime) are provided, and supplementary experiments with anisotropic covariates (Appendix A.2.2) qualitatively corroborate the theory.
The appendices are comprehensive, with self-contained proofs of all claims (Sections C-F), including auxiliary lemmas with explicit constant dependencies.
weaknesses: The conceptual core—the linearization of Gaussian-input softmax attention in the infinite-prompt limit—is not new (Vuckovic et al. 2020, Sander et al. 2022, Castin et al. 2025 are cited as such), the concentration results overlap with concurrent work (Bohbot et al. 2025), and Theorem 5.2 largely adapts Zhang et al. (2024). The novelty is thus in the packaging and the gradient-concentration/dynamics transfer, which is solid but incremental relative to these closely related works.

The main theorems are qualitative: Theorem 4.3 and 5.2 assert only the existence of a threshold L(ε) with no explicit rates, and the concentration bounds have implicit constants and slow poly(L^{-c}) rates. The authors acknowledge this, but it limits the practical guidance on how large prompts must be for the approximation to be meaningful.

There is a potential tension in the bound's dependence on parameters: the constants depend on ∥U∥op (and the concentration is uniform only over a ball B2ρ), while Theorem 4.3 assumes a priori that the infinite-prompt gradient flow remains confined to Bρ. This is a strong structural assumption that is verified only in the specific linear-regression setting via Zhang et al. (2024), so the 'general in-context learning' scope of Section 4 is narrower than it may appear.

The application inherits restrictive conditions: the small-initialization Assumption 5.1 (α small), the preserved block structure, i.i.d. tokens without positional encodings or masking, and single-layer attention. These are standard in this literature but confine relevance to stylized settings.

Experiments are small-scale (d = 5, ~30 min on a laptop) and primarily qualitative confirmations (convergence of outputs, gradients, and risks with L); no quantitative comparison against the theory's predicted rates is possible or attempted given the implicit constants.

Some presentation issues: Assumption 3.3/4.2(iii) moment conditions are stated somewhat abstractly and their verification for general sub-Gaussian distributions beyond Gaussian is not fully demonstrated; minor typos and duplicated phrasing appear in Appendix A.2.2.

strengths: The paper is built on a coherent and clearly stated framework: the measure-based view of attention (Vuckovic et al., 2020; Sander et al., 2022) is used to identify a limit in which softmax attention becomes linear for centered Gaussian inputs, and all main results flow logically from this observation.

The concentration analysis (Propositions 3.1 and 3.4) is technically non-trivial: softmax weights exp(z^T U z) are heavy-tailed under sub-Gaussian tokens, and the proof strategy (case split on the high-probability event where softmax terms are bounded, with convex-hull/max-inequality control on the complement) is a clean and reusable technique. The extension of the argument to gradients, and the general f, g formulation in Lemmas C.6/C.9, are a genuine toolkit contribution.

Theorem 5.2 extends convergence guarantees for in-context linear regression with softmax attention beyond isotropic covariates, relaxing a restriction of Chen et al. (2024), and provides an alternative, comparatively simpler proof route.

The numerical experiments (Figures 1-3, plus the anisotropic appendix experiments) qualitatively match the theoretical predictions, and the paper is honest about what the experiments show (e.g., softmax does not outperform linear attention in this toy setting).
weaknesses: Limited originality of the central insight. The key ingredient — softmax attention acting on the full Gaussian measure is linear (Lemma 2.1) — is explicitly imported from Castin et al. (2025), and the measure-based formulation is due to Vuckovic et al. (2020) and Sander et al. (2022). The contribution is largely a combination of these ingredients with a Gronwall argument, which diminishes the conceptual novelty.

Overlapping concurrent work is acknowledged but weakly differentiated: Bohbot et al. (2025) already establishes concentration of attention output in the large-prompt regime with sharper rates. The claimed added value (concentration of gradients, needed for training dynamics) is real but the incremental delta is modest.

The headline guarantees are purely qualitative. Theorem 4.3 and Theorem 5.2 provide no explicit rate for L(ε); the constants in Propositions 3.1/3.4 (e.g., L^{c2/σ^2} with c2 unspecified in the main text, and polylog factors with large σ exponents) make it impossible to assess whether the 'large-prompt regime' is anywhere near realistic prompt lengths. For a paper whose entire value proposition is the finite-to-infinite-prompt transfer, the absence of quantitative rates is a significant weakness.

Theorem 5.2 essentially re-derives, via transfer, a result already available in Chen et al. (2024) for the isotropic case; the genuinely new content (anisotropic extension) is the paper's most important claim but is supported only qualitatively and by toy experiments in Appendix A.2.2.

Restrictive assumptions are stacked for the application: Assumption 5.1 imposes a specific block initialization with small α, Σ must be invertible (degenerate case relegated to informal sketches in Appendix F.3), and the setting is single-layer, univariate output, Gaussian tokens only. The practical relevance of the transfer result is therefore narrow.

Experiments are minimal: d = 5, linear regression, a single anisotropic covariance matrix, ~30 minutes per run on a laptop. They confirm the theory in the easiest regime but do not probe the boundary of validity (e.g., non-Gaussian tokens, large dimension, task distributions outside the framework).
Reproducibility gap: Appendix A.1 states the code 'is publicly available at .' with the URL missing, so the code is effectively not accessible as submitted.

Presentation issues: duplicated/contradictory sentences in Appendix A.2.2 ('In this representative anisotropic setting, we observe...' followed by 'In this typical anisotropic case, we get similar observations...'), Remark 3.2 concedes that the analysis is performed for a fresh query token rather than the practically relevant self-attention setting with only informal justification, and there is no dedicated limitations discussion despite the Gaussian/i.i.d. assumptions being central caveats.

strengths: The paper develops a coherent, measure-based framework that unifies finite- and infinite-prompt softmax attention, and clearly identifies the regime (centered Gaussian tokens) in which softmax attention becomes analytically equivalent to linear attention.

The concentration results (Propositions 3.1 and 3.4) cover not only the attention output but also the gradients with respect to trainable parameters, which is the key technical ingredient enabling the training-dynamics transfer in Theorem 4.3. The proof sketches handle genuinely nontrivial obstacles (heavy-tailed softmax weights exp(z^T U z), averaging over query tokens) in a clean way.

Theorem 4.3 is a useful, general result: under mild assumptions (sub-Gaussian tokens, bounded trajectory), the finite-prompt gradient-flow risk is asymptotically bounded by the infinite-prompt risk, providing a principled bridge that lets existing linear-attention analyses transfer to softmax attention.

Theorem 5.2 gives, to my knowledge, the first convergence guarantee for in-context linear regression with softmax attention under anisotropic Gaussian covariates, improving on Chen et al. (2024), which is restricted to isotropic covariates and requires heavier machinery. The extension to degenerate covariance (Appendix F.3) is a nice bonus.

The numerical experiments (Sections 6 and Appendix A.2) directly illustrate each theoretical claim: output/gradient concentration, convergence of ICL risk to the Bayes level, and alignment of softmax and linear training trajectories, in both isotropic and anisotropic settings.

The paper is well organized and honestly discusses its limitations: no explicit convergence rates, the i.i.d./Gaussian assumption, the small-initialization condition of Assumption 5.1, and the concurrent work of Bohbot et al. (2025) are all candidly acknowledged.
Appendix proofs are detailed and self-contained, supporting reproducibility of the theoretical claims; experiments build on the public codebase of He et al. (2025).
weaknesses: The quantitative strength of the results is limited. The concentration rates ln(L)/L^{c2/sigma^2} depend on unspecified constants c2 that may be small, and the paper provides no explicit rates or finite-L guarantees beyond the qualitative existence of a threshold L(eps); Theorem 5.2 is thus an asymptotic-in-L statement. Practitioners get little quantitative guidance on how large L must be.

The central observation—softmax attention with Gaussian data converges to an affine/linear operator as L → infinity—is a fairly direct consequence of the law of large numbers (Lemma 2.1 is essentially known from Castin et al. 2025), so the paper's novelty rests on the gradient concentration and the dynamics-transfer argument rather than a fundamentally new phenomenon.

The result depends on the gradient flow staying in a compact ball (Theorem 4.3) and on small initialization alpha (Assumption 5.1); while the authors note this is mainly technical, it narrows the applicability of the training-dynamics guarantees.

The generality claim must be qualified: equivalence to linear attention holds only for centered Gaussian (or bounded) input measures. For non-Gaussian, non-centered, or structured (non-i.i.d.) data—which are the practically relevant cases for LLMs—the infinite-prompt limit is no longer linear, and the framework offers no quantitative guidance.

There is meaningful overlap with concurrent work: Bohbot et al. (2025) derives sharper output concentration in the same regime (the differentiation here—gradient concentration and training dynamics—is real but the Section 3 contribution is partially incremental), and Theorem 5.2's Bayes-optimality conclusion essentially follows by importing Zhang et al. (2024) with 'minor adaptations'.

Experiments are toy-scale (d = 5, single-layer, single-head, SGD on a laptop); they are appropriate as illustrations but do not test robustness of the theory at larger scale or under mild distributional misspecification (e.g., the effect of a nonzero mean, which is known to change the softmax limit).
A minor presentation/reproducibility issue: the code-availability line in Appendix A.1 reads 'publicly available at .' with no URL, which should be fixed.
